question: Into what three blocks of fourteen generations does Matthew organize the genealogy, and what women does he make a point of mentioning?
The verb γεννάω (gennao, “beget, be the father of”) is repeated throughout the list, but changes form in verse 16: what does this change indicate about Jesus' birth?
How does Joseph act regarding Mary's pregnancy before and after the dream, and what does the text mean by calling him “righteous”?
The name Immanuel means “God with us”: in what concrete situation do you need to remember this today?
Who seeks the child, where do they come from, how do they reach Him and what do they offer?
The verb προσκυνέω (proskyneo, “worship, bow down”) appears in the mouth of the Magi and in Herod's: what difference is there between the worship of the ones and that of the other?
What parallels with Israel's history, such as the going to and returning from Egypt, does Matthew seem to highlight in Jesus' childhood?
Herod and “all Jerusalem” are disturbed by the news of a king: what part of you feels threatened by the idea of Jesus reigning?
Where does John preach, how does he dress, what does he eat, and who comes to him?
The word μετάνοια (metanoia, “repentance, change of mind”) appears together with the idea of fruit: what does John expect to see in those who say they have repented?
Why does Jesus insist on being baptized by John, and what do the voice from heaven and the Spirit reveal about Him?
“We have Abraham as our father”: what might you be trusting in instead of a real change of life?
What are the three temptations in the wilderness, and with what words does Jesus answer each one?
The verb πειράζω (peirazo) can mean “tempt” and also “test, prove”: what difference does it make to read the wilderness one way or the other?
What similarities are there between Jesus' forty days in the wilderness and Israel's forty years in the wilderness, from which the quotations of Deuteronomy come?
Peter, Andrew, James and John leave nets, boat and father: what does following Jesus ask you to leave today?
What kinds of people does Jesus call “blessed,” and what promise goes with each one?
The word μακάριος (makarios, “blessed, happy”) opens each beatitude: what kind of happiness is this, if it includes those who mourn and the persecuted?
What does Jesus mean when He says He came to “fulfill” the Law and the Prophets, and how does this connect with the “you have heard... but I tell you” that follow?
What attitudes does Jesus ask for toward those who strike, take or compel, and how does verse 45 justify love of enemies?
Jesus tells us to leave the gift at the altar and first go be reconciled: with whom do you need to talk before going on?
What three religious practices does Jesus comment on, and what contrast does He draw in each between what is seen by people and what is done “in secret”?
The word ὑποκριτής (hypokrites) designated a stage actor, who wore a mask: what does this origin add to what Jesus criticizes in the “hypocrites”?
Why, after the Lord's Prayer, does Jesus come back precisely to the request about forgiveness?
What do the images of the treasure, the eye and the two masters have in common?
Looking at the birds and the lilies, what concrete worry of yours could you hand over today to the Father's care?
What similarities and what differences are there between the two houses of the final parable?
The verb κρίνω (krino, “judge”) opens the chapter: what kind of judgment does Jesus forbid, considering also the discernment asked for in verses 15 to 20?
What image of God does Jesus present by comparing the Father with a human father who gives his son bread?
What “beam” in your own eye may be getting in the way of how you see others?
Who are the three people healed at the beginning of the chapter, and what makes each one “out of the ordinary” for the society of the time?
The word πίστις (pistis, “faith”) appears in the praise of the centurion, and in verse 26 the disciples are called “of little faith”: what distinguishes one reaction from the other?
What cost of discipleship does Jesus show in His answers to the scribe and to the disciple who wanted to bury his father?
“Lord, save us!”: what storm in your life is making you doubt that Jesus cares?
How is Matthew called, who goes to dinner with Jesus at his house, and how do the Pharisees react?
The word ἔλεος (eleos, “mercy”) comes from Hosea 6:6: why does Jesus tell the Pharisees to “learn” what this phrase means?
What do the images of the bridegroom, the new patch and the new wine say about the newness Jesus brings?
Jesus sees the crowds “like sheep without a shepherd” and is moved with compassion: who around you is like this, and what could you do?
How are the stories of the synagogue leader's daughter and of the woman with the bleeding intertwined?
What instructions does Jesus give the Twelve about where to go, what to take and how to act in the houses?
The word ἀπόστολος (apostolos, “one who is sent”) appears only here in Matthew: how does the verb “send” in verses 5, 16 and 40 help us understand this title?
How should we understand that Jesus says He did not come to bring peace but a sword, and what does it mean to lose one's life in order to find it?
The sparrows and the numbered hairs speak of God's care: what fear of yours could this image touch?
What question does John send from prison, and with what facts does Jesus answer, without simply saying “yes”?
The verb σκανδαλίζω (skandalizo, “stumble, take offense”), translated here as “fall away,” speaks of a stone in the path: what in Jesus could make John or others stumble?
What does the comparison with the children in the marketplaces reveal about that generation's reaction to John and to Jesus?
Jesus offers rest to those who are weary and burdened: what weight are you carrying today, and what would it be like to exchange it for the “easy yoke”?
What two Sabbath situations provoke conflict with the Pharisees, and how does Jesus respond in each?
The word σάββατον (sabbaton, “Sabbath”) is repeated at the beginning of the chapter: what does Jesus show about the purpose of the Sabbath by speaking of David, the priests and the sheep in the pit?
Why is attributing Jesus' work to Beelzebul so serious, and what does the image of the strong man bound teach about the Kingdom?
How does Jesus redefine His family when His mother and brothers look for Him?
“A bruised reed He will not break”: how do you treat those around you who are fragile or almost snuffed out?
Where do the seeds fall in the parable of the sower, and what happens to each part?
The word παραβολή (parabole, “parable, comparison”) marks the whole chapter: according to verses 10 to 17, why does Jesus speak this way to the crowds?
What does the parable of the weeds teach about the coexistence of good and evil until the end, and about who has the right to separate them?
What do the hidden treasure and the pearl of great value have in common, and what reaction do they provoke in those who find them?
What “thorns,” such as worry and the deceitfulness of wealth, may be choking the word in your life?
Why was John arrested, and what sequence of events at Herod's feast leads to his death?
What contrast does Matthew create between Herod's banquet and Jesus' meal with the crowd in the desolate place?
The verb διστάζω (distazo, “doubt, waver”) appears in the question to Peter: what makes Peter begin to sink, according to verse 30?
“You give them something to eat”: in the face of a great need, what “five loaves and two fish” do you have to hand to Jesus?
Of what do the Pharisees and scribes accuse the disciples, and what example does Jesus use to turn the accusation back on them?
The verb κοινόω (koinoo, “make common, defile”) is repeated in Jesus' explanation: where, according to Him, does what truly defiles a person come from?
How should we understand the harsh dialogue between Jesus and the Canaanite woman, and what does her answer reveal?
“These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me”: at what moments could this describe your own faith?
What opinions about Jesus were going around among the people, and what does Peter answer when the question is put directly to the disciples?

The word ἐκκλησία (ekklesia, “assembly, church”) appears here for the first time in the Gospels, beside the play between Πέτρος (Petros) and πέτρα (petra): how do the Christian traditions read this verse?
Why is Peter, right after being called “blessed,” called “Satan” and a “stumbling block”?
Denying yourself and taking up your cross: what would this mean, concretely, in the week ahead of you?
Who goes up the mountain with Jesus, who appears beside Him, and what does the voice from the cloud command?
The verb μεταμορφόω (metamorphoo, “be transformed, be transfigured”) describes what happens to Jesus: what does this change reveal to the three disciples?
Why can the disciples not heal the boy, and what does Jesus want to teach with the image of the mustard seed?
Jesus touches the disciples who have fallen in fear and says “get up”: what fear of yours needs to hear this word today?
What question do the disciples ask, and what does Jesus do before answering?
The verb ἀφίημι (aphiemi, “forgive, release, let go”) runs through the end of the chapter: what does the idea of “letting go” add to our understanding of forgiveness?
What steps does Jesus propose when someone sins against another, and what goal appears in verse 15?
What contrast is there between the debt of ten thousand talents and that of a hundred denarii, and what does this contrast want to show?
Peter asks “how many times?”: who are you counting the times you have had to forgive?
